1.problem:
There are 2026 integers greater than 1 written on a blackboard, not necessarily different. In a move, Confucius chooses two integers \(m > 1\) and \(n > 1\) from different places on the blackboard and replaces the two integers with

\[\gcd(m,n) \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)}{\gcd(m,n)}.\]

He continues to make moves while it is possible to do so.

(a). Prove that, regardless of the choices of Confucius, after finitely many moves, exactly one integer \(M\) on the blackboard is greater than 1.

(b). Prove that the value of \(M\) does not depend on the choices of Confucius.

(Note that \(\gcd(x,y)\) denotes the greatest common divisor of positive integers \(x\) and \(y\), and \(\operatorname{lcm}(x,y)\) denotes the least common multiple of \(x\) and \(y\).)
1.solutions:
Solution 1

Say we remove one element, call it \(e\). Form the \(45 \times 45\) matrix and call it our blackboard \(\mathcal{B}\). At each step, choose two \(m,n > 1\) such that they are replaced in \(\mathcal{B}\) to

\[\gcd(m,n)\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)}{\gcd(m,n)}=\frac{mn}{\gcd(m,n)^2}\] .

Let \(g = \gcd(m,n)\).

Lemma 1: The 2025 elements in the matrix have the property that they will never degenerate to a case where all elements are 1.

Proof of Lemma 1:

Suppose two entries \(m,n > 1\) are inserted. Then, they are replaced by \(g\) and \(\frac{mn}{g^2}\). Assume that both replacements degenerate to 1. Then \(g = 1\) from which \(mn\) is the remaining. But \(m,n > 1\) hence this is impossible. So at least one element after this process is greater than 1.

Lemma 2: Suppose \(\mathcal{B}\) contains \(k \geq 1\) elements greater than 1. If \(e > 1\) is the removed element, then adding back \(e\) and performing the same moveset as above degenerates the new blackboard to a case where exactly one element is greater than 1.

Proof of Lemma 2:

Let \(a,b > 1\) be two numbers in \(k\). Consider their prime factorizations. For any prime \(p\) let \(v_p(a)\) and \(v_p(b)\) be the power of \(p\) in \(a,b\) respectively. The moveset replaces the values with \(\min(v_p(a),v_p(b))\) and \(|v_p(a)-v_p(b)|\). However, this is just the Euclidean algorithm on the exponents of any given prime in \(a,b\). The algorithm always ends with a nonzero value and one zero value for \(v_p(a,b)\). Hence, one of the numbers is greater than one and the other is one itself. Therefore, exactly one number exists that is greater than 1.

2026 IMO Q1 Part A:

Lemma 2 proves the result. \(\square\)

We now prove that \(e\) is invariant and no matter what we choose the value of \(e\) to be in the original 2026 matrix, the result always holds.

Lemma 3: \(\gcd\bigl(v_p(a_1),v_p(a_2),\dots,v_p(a_n)\bigr)\) is invariant under any move.

Proof of Lemma 3:

If Confucius chooses \(m\) and \(n\), then let \(x=v_p(m), y=v_p(n)\). These moves replace \(m\) and \(n\) by \(\gcd(m,n), \frac{\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)}{\gcd(m,n)}\). By Lemma 2, that is \(\min(x,y)\) and \(|x-y|\). In Lemma 2, we also showed this is the Euclidean Algorithm. Hence, \(\gcd(x,y)=\gcd(\min(x,y),|x-y|)\), which is the same greatest common factor. Extending to \(n\) such integers, the result follows.

2026 IMO Q1 Part B:

By Lemma 2 exactly one number \(M\) remains and all others are 1. Thus \(\gcd(M,1,1,\dots,1)=M\). In addition, the greatest common factor of all numbers on the blackboard is just \(\prod_{p} p^{v_{p}(M)} = M\). However, by Lemma 3 \(p^{v_{p}(M)}\) for all \(p\) is invariant hence \(M\) is invariant. \(\square\)

~Pinotation

Remark

Honestly this was a really good problem, especially for a question 1. Its approach is clever, and its usage of \(v_p\) really simplify the blackboard. The fact one can just remove an element to form a perfect square too is clever, so such a great problem for the IMO. :>

Solution 2

Part a: Assume FTSOC, Confucius is able to do infinite moves. Now, if we turn a number into \(1\), \(2025\) times, we can’t do any more moves, so we can turn a number into \(1\) at most \(2024\) times. Thus, there must be an infinite number of moves that don’t turn a number into \(1\), which means an infinite number of moves where \(\gcd(m, n) > 1\). For each of these infinite moves, the product of the numbers goes from \(mn\) to \(\frac{mn}{\gcd(m, n)}\). Thus, the product decreases, but it can’t decrease for an infinite number of moves while staying a positive integer, so we are done. \(M>1\) follows from the fact that the \(\gcd(m, n)\) and \(\frac{\text{lcm}(m, n)}{\gcd(m. n)}\) can’t both be \(1\) unless both \(m=n=1\).

Part b: Assume FTSOC, we start with \(a_1, a_2, ..., a_n\) and Confucius can end with \(M=x\) or \(M=y\). Since \(x \neq y\), there must be a prime \(p\) such that \(v_px=a\) and \(v_py=b\) where \(a, b\) are nonnegative distinct integers. Now, we will consider the exponents of \(p\) in the \(a_i\), to form a new sequence, \(b_i\). Now, Confucius’s operation turns \(2\) numbers, \(m, n\) in \(b_i\) to \(m, n-m\) when \(n \geq m\). Since Confucius’s operations in \(a_i\) end with all \(1\)s and \(M\), we have that in \(b_i\), his operations and with all \(0\)s and either \(a\) or \(b\). We see that turning \(m, n\) to \(m, n-m\) when \(n \geq m\) keeps the gcd constant. Since we must end up with all \(0\)s and \(a\) or \(b\), we have \(\gcd(0, 0, ..., 0, a)=gcd(0, 0, ..., 0, b)\) or just \(a=b\) and we are done.

~Math645

Solution 3

We can look at every prime separately. Let \(\mathbf{v}\) be a list of \(n=2026\) registers initialized to the powers of \(p\) in the list on the blackboard. A move sends

\[(v_i,v_j)\mapsto (|v_i-v_j|, \min(v_i, v_j))\]

This is exactly one step in the the Euclidean algorithm, which runs until the terminal state \((0, \gcd(v_i, v_j))\). The proof the Euclidean algorithm works is the same as the proof Confucius will end up at

\[(0, 0, \dots, \gcd(\mathbf{v})).\]

The algorithm is a semi-invariant: at least one register gets smaller with each step, and no register gets larger. There is always another step until the terminal

\[(0, 0, \dots, \text{something})\]

There is also an invariant in this algorithm: \(\gcd(\mathbf{v})\) remains constant at every step. Since \(\gcd(0, 0, \dots, \text{something}) = \text{something}\) that terminal \(\text{something}\) must be the greatest common divisor of the original registers.

Exponentiating from the \(v_p\) setting to any product of primes gives the terminal

\[(1, 1, \dots, \prod_{p\text{ prime}}p^{\gcd(\mathbf{v_p})})\]

2.problem:
Let \(ABC\) be a triangle and let points \(M\) and \(N\) be the midpoints of sides \(AB\) and \(AC\), respectively. Let points \(K\) and \(L\) be chosen strictly inside triangles \(BMC\) and \(BNC\), respectively, such that \(K\) lies strictly inside triangle \(ABL\) and \(L\) lies strictly inside triangle \(AKC\). Suppose that

\[\angle KBA = \angle ACL, \quad \angle LBK = \angle LNC, \quad \angle LCK = \angle BMK.\]

Let \(O\) be the circumcentre of triangle \(AKL\). Prove that

\[OM = ON.\]
2.solutions:
Video Solution

https://youtu.be/QDmEhFgBb8M (by Dedekind Cuts)

Solution 1

Let \(D\) be the circumcentre of \(\triangle AMN\).

Lemma 1: \(MN \parallel KL\).

Proof of the Lemma 1:

By definition \(OK = OL\). Let the midpoint of \(KL\) be \(F\). Note that \(O\) lies on the perpendicular line through \(F\) of \(KL\). Also, point \(D\) lies on the perpendicular line through the midpoint of \(MN\), say \(H\), of line \(MN\). Note that then the intersections of both lines upon \(MN\) and \(KL\) are \(I\) and \(J\) respectively, it follows that \(HIJF\) is a rectangle. Hence, \(MN \parallel KL\), as desired.

Lemma 2: \(D\) and \(O\) are collinear along the perpendicular bisector of \(KL\).

Proof of Lemma 2:

We prove that \(MN\) and \(KL\) share a common perpendicular bisector.

Note that the two circles who circumscribe \(AMN\) and \(AKL\), say \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) respectively, are common at \(A\). Also, as their bases \(MN\) and \(KL\) are parallel by Lemma 1, then \(MKNL\) is a trapezoid through homothety about \(A\). By definition, \(MNCB\) is also a trapezoid. Funny enough, the facts \(\angle KBA = \angle ACL, \angle LBK = \angle LNC, \angle LCK = \angle BMK\) along with the fact \(MKNL\) is a trapezoid completes the topmost angle measures of the original trapezoid, hence it is given \(MNCB \sim MKNL\). Extend \(MK\) past \(K\) and \(NL\) past \(L\) to intersect at \(Q\) and \(R\) respectively. Angle chasing given the constraints of the problem shows that \(MKNL \sim MQRN\). This result could elegantly be obtained through a homothety on \(A\) along \(\Omega\), which is the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABC\). However, both trapezoids also share a base, hence they must also share a similar perpendicular bisector, which indeed proves \(D\) and \(O\) are collinear along the bisector of \(KL\).

2026 IMO Q2

Given Lemma 2 it is obvious that \(\angle MHD = \angle MHO = 90^\circ\). Given the fact that \(H\) is the midpoint, it follows through converse the definition of isosceles triangles that \(OM = ON\). \(\square\)

~Pinotation

Remark

For Lemma 2, it is also possible to show the trapezoids must share a common perpendicular bisector by the mutual power of points and Miquel configurations associated with the three given angle equations. It is also possible to apply Radical Axis Theorem to skip the purpose of Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 entirely and elegantly obtain the exact result without the angle chasing brute force of doom in this solution. That solution is dedicated to @dedekindcuts (video solution)

3.problem:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer.

Liu Bang and Xiang Yu have a stick of side length 1 and want to divide it between themselves. Liu marks at most \(n\) points on the stick, and then Xiang marks at most \(n\) points on the stick. The marked points are distinct. Then, the stick is cut at all marked points, creating a number of pieces. Afterwards, they take turns claiming any unclaimed piece of the stick, with Liu going first. Each player’s goal is to maximize the total length of their own pieces.

For each \(n\), determine the largest value of \(c\) such that Liu may guarantee a total length of at least \(c\), regardless of Xiang’s play.
3.solutions:
Video Solution

https://youtu.be/pfi6DWlXyrI (including motivation discussion, by Dedekind Cuts)

Solution 1

Let each of the partitioned sticks be of length \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2n}\), in decreasing order, as \(a_1 \geq a_2 \geq \dots \geq a_{2n}\). Note that then, Liu always takes \(a_1, a_3, \dots, a_{2n-1}\). Hence, we must find the minimum of

\[\sum_{1 \leq i = \text{odd} < 2n} a_i\] .

Lemma 1: Liu guarantees maximality when taking sticks in a geometric progression of common ratio \(\frac{1}{2^{n+1} -1}\).

Proof of Lemma 1:

Liu wants to partition the sticks such that no matter where or how he cuts the larger stick, he can still obtain a net growth. Suppose he creates a cut of two sticks \(A < B\). Now, if Xiang leaves \(B\) uncut, Liu will grab \(B\) first. Otherwise, if he cuts \(B\), the worst possible case is that he cuts it into direct halves. To not render \(B\) useless, Liu can cut \(B\) into double that of \(A\), hence it is a net gain greater than or equal to 0. But the thing is, if we have only \(A\) and \(B\) as our leading sticks, with \(B\) double that of \(A\), then three new sticks are formed after Xiang cuts, from which by Pigeonhole Principle, Liu obtains the last stick, hence winning the game.

We can guarantee that doubling is the best possible strategy for Liu. If he were to cut triple of quadruple that into pieces \(A\) and \(B\), Xiang can make some number of cuts with \(n\) cuts such that all pieces are useless in comparison to \(A\). (Indeed, with the max length 1, there is more than enough \(n\) to pass around, as you can check via the base cases.)

So, via the doubling strategy, each of the sticks have lengths \(\delta(1, 2, 4, \dots, 2^n)\). Here, \(\delta\) is our common ratio. This inner sum is \(2^{n+1}-1\). Then, \(\delta(2^{n+1} -1) = 1\) hence \(\delta = \frac{1}{2^{n+1} -1}\), as desired.

Lemma 2: Regardless of Xiang’s plays, Liu can guarantee \(\frac{2^n}{2^{n+1} -1}\) of minimum length.

Proof of Lemma 2:

Suppose he were to make these cuts in the common ratio found in Lemma 1. Then, given such \(n+1\) cuts, the only plausible moveset that Xiang could play is to split all given segments in half. That is, he MUST split the larger \(n\) segments in half, whereas the last segment of length 1 is as desired. Then, Liu obtains all odd numbered lengths when ordered \(a_1 \rightarrow a_n\) in decreased order, which is \(\delta(1+1+2+4+\dots+2^{n-1}) = \delta(2^n - 1 + 1)= \delta \cdot 2^n\), which implies the length \(\frac{2^n}{2^{n+1} - 1}\), as desired.

2026 IMO Q3:

We denote \(c\) to be the minimum length regardless of Xiang’s plays. If we prove that Xiang plays optimally yet we still obtain a minimum length, then we may guarantee that Liu obtains a length greater than or equal to this minimum by definition. That is, through Lemma 2,

\[c = \boxed{\frac{2^n}{2^{n+1} - 1}} \quad \square\]

~Pinotation

Solution 2

We claim that the answer is \(\frac{2^n}{2^{n+1} - 1}\). First, we will show that Xiang can always guarantee a length for themself of at least \(\frac{2^n-1}{2^{n+1} - 1}\). If Liu does not use all \(n\) marks, then Xiang can simply bisect each segment resulting from Liu’s marks, and Xiang will end up with a length of \(1/2\). Say then that Liu does use all \(n\) marks, resulting in \(n+1\) lengths. We assume that Xiang cuts the stick at all of the points Liu marks before making their own marks.

Consider the \(2^{n+1}\) sums of subsets of these lengths. Since each sum is in \([0,1]\), two of these sums will have difference at most \(\frac{1}{2^{n+1} - 1}\). Say that these sums correspond to subsets \(J,K\subset[n+1]\). Xiang may perform the following procedure:

  • Draw a vertical line in the sand.
  • Take all of the pieces in \(J\setminus(J\cap K)\) and line them up horizontally end to end, making one continuous segment of pieces, so that the left end of the first stick touches the line.
  • Take all of the pieces in \(K\setminus(J\cap K)\) and line them up in the same fashion, just below the first set of sticks.
  • At any \(x\)-value where one segment has a break and the other segment does not, mark the other segment at that \(x\)-value. Note that the number of marks made will be at most one less than the number of the sticks which have been placed in the sand.
  • For every piece not placed in the sand (those in \([n+1]\setminus(J\cup K)\)), mark them in their center.

At the end of this process, there will be \(n\) pairs of pieces which are the same length, and one piece which has length at most \(\frac{1}{2^{n+1} - 1}\). We claim that this guarantees a length for Xiang of at least \(\frac{2^n-1}{2^{n+1} - 1}\). To prove this:

  • Draw a vertical line in the sand.
  • Line up all of the pieces of sticks from largest to smallest, such that for each stick its left end touches the vertical line.
  • Below all of the pieces of sticks, add a ruler whose left end aligns with the vertical line.
  • As Liu and Xiang take pieces, if Liu’s piece is larger than Xiangs, or if Liu is taking the last piece, cover the piece of the ruler with tape from the length of Xiang’s piece to the length of Liu’s piece.

Note that in this process, the total length of tape will be at most the length of our un-paired piece, proving our first part of the claim.

Now say that Liu marks the stick so that the resulting pieces would have lengths \(\frac{2^k}{2^{n+1} - 1}\) for \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). We wish to show that Xiang cannot make marks so as to guarantee a length for themself of more than \(\frac{2^n-1}{2^{n+1} - 1}\). We will compute a slightly different value. In particular, it is equivalent to show that

\[1-(\text{Liu's length} - \text{Xiang's length})\]

is at most \(\frac{2^{n+1}-2}{2^{n+1} - 1}\). There is a simple way of calculating this value. Once the stick has been marked by both players and cut, we can say that they take their pieces of the stick simultaneously. When they are each holding their piece, we can take two pieces of tape, each the length of the shorter of the two pieces of sticks being held, and place one piece of tape on each piece of stick. If only Liu has a piece of stick, as there were an odd number of pieces of stick to begin with and this is the last one, we do not place any tape. The total of the lengths of these pieces of tape will be the value we seek. We say that each pair of pieces of tape has its own unique shared color.

Now say that after placing these pieces of tape, we perform the following simple procedure:

  • Re-arrange the pieces of the stick so that they are where they were before the markings were made, making one continuous segment of pieces.
  • At each of Liu’s markings, separate the segment of pieces into two segments of pieces.

Now we have \(n+1\) segments of pieces of sticks, of lengths \(\frac{2^k}{2^{n+1} - 1}\) for \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), upon which there are \(n\) pairs of pieces of tape. Take each segment which has two pieces of tape of the same color and set it aside. Say that \(k\) segments remain, noting that \(k>0\). On them, at most \(k\) colors of tape will remain, and for each color, there will be at most two pieces of tape, and if there are two, then they will be on different segments. Consider then how much of the longest remaining segment can be covered in tape. Indeed, no more than the sum of the lengths of the other remaining segments. Thus, at least \(\frac{1}{2^{n+1} - 1}\) of that segment will not be covered in tape, proving that the total length of tape is at most \(\frac{2^{n+1}}{2^{n+1} - 1}\). We are done.

~flyingpurplepeopleeater

4.problem:
Shan-Yu and Mulan are playing a game. Let \(\theta\) be an angle with \(0^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ\) known to both players. Initially, Shan-Yu makes a paper triangle \(\mathcal{T}\) with measurements of his choice. They repeatedly form the following steps.

  • If \(\mathcal{T}\) has at least one angle measuring exactly \(\theta\), then the game stops and Mulan wins.
  • Otherwise, Mulan chooses a point \(P\) on the perimeter of \(\mathcal{T}\), different from its three vertices. She then makes a straight cut from \(P\) to the opposite vertex of \(\mathcal{T}\).
  • Shan-Yu discards one of the two triangles. The remaining triangle becomes the new \(\mathcal{T}\).

For which real values of \(\theta\) can Mulan guarantee her victory in finitely many steps, no matter how Shan-Yu plays?
4.solutions:
Solution 1

I claim that Mulan must always choose the angle \(\theta = \boxed{\frac{180^\circ}{n}}\) for any integer \(n \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 2}^+\).

We assume both Shan-Yu and Mulan play optimally. Suppose that the original triangle \(\mathcal{T}_0\) has angles \(A,B,C\), none of which is \(\theta\). We consider all possible cases of triangles, acute, right, or obtuse.

Lemma: The optimal strategy for Mulan is to choose points such that she splits the triangle into two that of \(\theta\).

Proof of the Lemma:

If she were to choose a point that is of the properties of Lemma 1, then no matter what triangle Shan-Yu counters, Mulan may always pick the remaining triangle.

2026 IMO/Q4:

We now must find all viable theta. If we are able to win against Shan-Yu, then we must come from a direct multiple of \(\theta\), meaning that one of \(A,B,C\) is a multiple of \(\theta\). This can be quite easily proven. Assume \(A = n\theta\) for some \(n\). If \(n\) is odd, then Mulan may choose a point such that we cut \(A\) into \((n-1)\theta\) and \(\theta\), in which the result follows from Lemma 1. Otherwise, \(n\) being even is trivial. So, if for some \(k \in \mathbb{Z}^+\) exists and Mulan can obtain it, such a solution is possible.

Now, if Shan-Yu chooses the initial triangle, he will obviously not choose one with \(\theta\) as an angle. However, his angles must sum to 180 degrees. If \(180 = k\theta\) for some value of \(k\), then Shan-Yu will lose, because if the angle measures of \(\mathcal{T}\) are \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\), then \(x+y+z = 180 = k\theta\) implies that for some placement of points within the triangle, Mulan can form an angle alongside the second line connecting a vertex to a point of her choosing, which yields 180 degrees universally, by precisely choosing a point such that the resulting angles formed are perfect multiples of \(\theta\).

From there, she may repeatedly apply the Lemma to win the game.

Thus, Mulan must always choose the angle \(\theta = \boxed{\frac{180^\circ}{n}}\) for any integer \(n \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 2}^+\). Note that \(n \geq 2\) due to the fact that the triangle in question is nondegenerate.

~Pinotation

Remark

What happens when 180 isn’t a multiple of \(\theta\)? Then, she can never apply the Lemma as Shan-Yu will just remove the angled triangle as he will never form a triangle whose angles are multiple measures of \(\theta\). In addition, as it isn’t an integer or nonintegral divisor of 180, she may never form two multiples of \(\theta\) via a 180 degree angle. Hence, she is at a checkmate, and once again, Shan-Yu, the ruthless leader of the Hun Army, terrorizes the land of math once more.

5.problem:
Let \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) be the set of all positive real numbers. Determine all functions \(f : \mathbb{R}_{>0} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{>0}\) such that

\[\sqrt{\frac{x^2 + f(y)^2}{2}} \geq \frac{f(x)+y}{2} \geq \sqrt{xf(y)}\]

for every \(x,y \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}\).
5.solutions:
Video Solution

https://youtu.be/Gmog2rVMNE4 (by Dedekind Cuts)

Solution 1

By the QM-AM-GM inequality, as long as \(f(x)+y=f(y)+x\) holds for every \(x,y\in\mathbb R_{>0}\), the original inequality holds.

Lemma 1: If and only if \(f(x)+y=f(y)+x\) hold for all non-negative \(x\) and \(y\),

\[\sqrt{\frac{x^2+f(y)^2}{2}}\ge \frac{f(x)+y}{2}\ge \sqrt{xf(y)}\]

holds.

Proof of Lemma 1:

Let \(x=f(y)\),

\[f(y)\ge \frac{f(f(y))+y}{2}\ge f(y).\]

So,

\[2f(y)-y=f(f(y)).\]

Let \(f(a)=f(b)\).

\[f(f(a))=f(f(b))=2f(a)-a=2f(b)-b.\]

So, \(a=b\), hence \(f\) is injective.

Let \(g(x)=f(x)-x\).

As long as \(f(x)\) is not in the form \(f(x)=x+b\), \(g(x)\) is injective.

First assume \(g(x)\) is injective. According to \(2f(y)-y=f(f(y))\),

\[g(f(x))=g(x).\]

Since \(g(x)\) is injective,

\[f(x)=x.\]

Then assume \(f(x)\) is in the form \(x+b\),

\[g(x)=b \text{ holds for all } x,\]

which means \(g(f(x))=g(x)\) holds for all non-negative \(b\) and \(x\).

Therefore, Combining the two assumptions,

\[\boxed{f(x)=x+b\quad \text{for all }b\ge0.}\]

Which also satisfies the lemma \(f(x)+y=f(y)+x\)

Solution 2

Motivation:

The LHS is just the Root Mean Squared of the MHS, which is then the AM-GM in comparison of the RHS. Hence we guess it is sufficient to find all functions that satisfy \(f(x)+y=f(y)+x\) for every \(x,y \in \mathbb R_{>0}\).

Lemma 1: If the given inequality holds then \(f(x)+y=f(y)+x\) also holds for every \(x,y \in \mathbb R_{>0}\).

Proof of the Lemma 1:

By the first pair of the Mean Inequality Chain, commonly denoted RMS-AM-GM-HM, specifically RMS-AM inequality, we have that

\[\sqrt{\frac{x^2 + f(y)^2}{2}} \geq \frac{f(y)+x}{2}\]

However, it is also given that

\[\sqrt{\frac{x^2 + f(y)^2}{2}} \geq \frac{f(x)+y}{2}\]

Hence either one value is greater than, one value is less than, or both values are equal to one another.

However, applying AM-GM on both, it is given that

\[\frac{f(x)+y}{2} \geq \sqrt{xf(y)}\]

and

\[\frac{f(y)+x}{2} \geq \sqrt{xf(y)}\] .

Because both share the same inequality as a lower bound, the converse of AM-GM proves that the two values must be equal. Hence,

\[\frac{f(x)+y}{2} = \frac{f(y)+x}{2} \implies f(x)+y = f(y)+x,\]

as desired.

Lemma 2: All such functions \(f(x) = x+c\) for a constant \(c \in \mathbb{R}^+ \cup 0\).

Proof of the Lemma 2:

Rearrange to obtain

\[f(x) - x = f(y)- y\] .

Now, because \(f(x) - x = f(y)- y = c\) for some constant \(c\), it is evident that \(f(x) = x+c\). We now prove that \(c\) must be nonnegative. However, by definition \(f : \mathbb{R}_{>0} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{>0}\), hence for the sake of contradiction assume that \(c < 0\) and choose an \(x\) such that \(0 < x < -c\). Then, \(f(x) = x+c < 0\) which is a contradiction, hence \(c \geq 0\), as desired.

2026 IMO/Q5:

Given the conditions, all functions \(\boxed{f(x) = x + c \ : \ c \geq 0}\) satisfy the result. \(\square\)

~Pinotation

Solution 3

Taking \(x\) to be \(f(y)\), we get

\[f(y)\geq \frac{f(f(y))+y}{2}\geq f(y)\]

Therefore,

\[f(f(y))=2f(y)-y\]

This is the same as \(f(f(x))-f(x)=f(x)-x\), which means that \(x_n=f^{n}(x_0)\) are arithmetic progressions with increment \(f(x_0)-x_0\) that must not be negative. Otherwise, \(x_n\) eventually would become negative.

Define \(g(x)=f(x)-x\). Note that \(g(x_n)=g(x_0)\). Then, from the second given inequality

\[(x+g(x)+y)^2\geq 4x(y+g(y))\]

Plugging in \(x_n\) for \(x\) and \(y_n=f^n(y_0)\) for \(y\), we get

\[(x_n+g(x_0)+y_m)^2\geq 4x_n(y_m+g(y_0))\]

or

\[(x_n-y_n)^2+2(x_n+y_m)g(x_0)+g(x_0)^2\geq 4x_ng(y_0)\]

For every large \(M\), since \(x_n\) and \(y_m\) are arithmetic progressions of increments \(g(x_0)\) and \(g(y_0)\), respectively, one can choose \(n\) and \(m\) such that \(|M-x_n|\leq g(x_0)\) and \(|M-y_m|\leq g(y_0)\). So, we get

\[(g(x_0)-g(y_0))^2+2(2M+g(x_0)+g(y_0))g(x_0)+g(x_0)\geq 4(M-g(x_0))g(y_0)\]

For this inequality to hold for arbitrarily large \(M\) one must have \(g(x_0)\geq g(y_0)\). Reversing the roles of \(x_n\) and \(y_m\) we get also \(g(y_0)\geq g(x_0)\). Therefore,

\[g(x_0)=g(y_0)\] .

It follows that \[f(x)=x+c\] , for some constant \(c\geq0\). One can check that all of these functions satisfy the inequalities.

6.problem:
Let \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots\) be an infinite sequence of positive integers greater than 1.

Suppose that for all positive integers \(n\), the number \(a_{n+1}\) is the smallest positive integer greater than \(a_n\) such that \(\gcd(a_{n+1}, a_i) > 1\) for every \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n\).

Prove that there exist positive integers \(T\) and \(L\) such that

\[a_{n+T} = a_n + L\]

for every positive integer \(n\).

(Note that \(\gcd(x,y)\) denotes the greatest common divisor of positive integers \(x\) and \(y\).)
6.solutions:
Video Solution

https://youtu.be/VyaOJAzIwbQ (by Dedekind Cuts)

Solution 1

Lemma 1: For all \(n\) the set of prime divisors of each of \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) is a fixed finite set.

Proof of Lemma 1:

Let \(P_n\) be the set of all prime numbers that divide at least one of \(a_1, \dots, a_n\). If such an \(a_{n+1}\) exists, \(a_{n+1}\) must share at least one common prime divisor with every previous term. That implies \( ext{a prime in} \ a_{n+1} \ \in P_n\). Notice that \(a_{n+1}\) however is minimalistic, hence if such a sequence \(a\) were to exist, by the Pigeonhole Principle, eventually new primes will no longer be introduced hence we "cycle" primes within each next term of \(a\). Hence there exists a set \(\mathcal{P} = \{p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k\}\) of finite prime divisors of \(a\) for all \(n\).

Lemma 2: If an integer \(x \in a\) works, then \(x + M \in a\) also works, where \(M = \prod \mathcal{P}\).

Proof of Lemma 2:

Denote \(M = p_1p_2\dots p_n\). If the term \(x \in a\) works, it has some prime factorization from which one value in the general prime pool \(M\) works. Then, we may simply factor this (or these) primes out, yielding a new number \(x+M\) who also satisfies the properties for some \(n\).

2026 IMO/Q6:

Suppose \(a_n\) is in this set \(a\). Consider \(L = M\), and notice that \(a_n + L\) is also in this set. Obviously, as \(L > 0\) and \(a_n + L > a_n\), it follows that then \(a_n+L\) occurs later in the sequence than \(a_n\). If this number appears exactly \(T\) later in the sequence, then it follows all elements of sequence \(a\) satisfy

\[a_{n+T} = a_n + L\]

for some integers \(T\) and \(L\). \(\square\)

~Pinotation

Remark

Quite a hard problem, living up to the ideal Q6 standards. Great problem to end the 2026 IMO. :>

As for the problem, notice that the next term \(a_{n+1}\) is determined solely based on the prime divisors of each of \(a_1, \dots, a_n\). This proof is left as an exercise to the reader.

Solution 2

Let

\[\mathcal{A} = \{a_1, a_2, \dots\}, \quad P(m) = \{ ext{all prime factors of } m\}.\]

By the recurrence condition, any two terms in the sequence are not coprime, i.e.

\[i eq j \implies P(a_i) \cap P(a_j) eq \emptyset. ag{1}\]

If an integer \(m \ge a_1\) does not belong to \(\mathcal{A}\), take \(k\) such that

\[a_k < m < a_{k+1}.\]

By the minimality of \(a_{k+1}\), there must be some \(i \le k\) such that \(\gcd(m, a_i) = 1\). Hence

\[m otin \mathcal{A} \implies \exists a_i < m, \quad P(m) \cap P(a_i) = \emptyset. ag{2}\]

From this we obtain an important property: if \(x \in \mathcal{A}\), \(m \ge a_1\), and \(P(x) \subseteq P(m)\), then

\[m \in \mathcal{A}. ag{3}\]

Otherwise, by (2) there exists \(a_i\) coprime to \(m\), hence coprime to \(x\), contradicting (1).

Now examine \(a_1, a_2, \dots\) in order and select "key terms": first select \(a_1\); if previously no key term \(b\) satisfies

\[P(b) \subseteq P(a_n),\]

then select \(a_n\). Clearly, every term \(a_n\) contains all prime factors of some key term.

We now prove that there are only finitely many key terms. Let

\[Q = P(a_1), \quad q_0 = \max Q, \quad C = a_1 q_0.\]

Suppose a key term \(x > C\) contains a prime factor \(p\) that has never appeared in any previous key term. Since \(a_1\) is a previous key term, \(p otin Q\). Also, since \(\gcd(x, a_1) > 1\), we can take

\[q \in P(x) \cap Q, \quad q eq p.\]

Let

\[S = P(x) \setminus \{p\}, \quad r = \prod_{i \in S} i.\]

For any previous key term \(b\), by (1) we have \(P(b) \cap P(x) eq \emptyset\); since \(p otin P(b)\), we get

\[P(b) \cap S eq \emptyset. ag{4}\]

Every previous term contains all prime factors of some previous key term, so any integer whose set of prime factors is \(S\) is not coprime to any term before \(x\). If \(r \ge a_1\), take \(y = r\). Since \(rp \mid x\), we have

\[a_1 \le y = r < x.\]

If \(r < a_1\), take the smallest positive integer \(t\) such that

\[y = rq^t \ge a_1.\]

Since \(rq^{t-1} < a_1\), we have

\[a_1 \le y = rq^t < qa_1 \le qa_1 = C < x.\]

So in both cases we have

\[a_1 \le y < x, \quad P(y) = S. ag{5}\]

By (4), \(y\) is not coprime to any term before \(x\); by (2), we have \(y \in \mathcal{A}\). Hence \(y\) contains all prime factors of some previous key term \(b\), so

\[P(b) \subseteq P(y) = S \subseteq P(x),\]

contradicting that \(x\) is a key term.

Therefore, no key term greater than \(C\) can introduce a new prime factor. There are only finitely many key terms not exceeding \(C\); let their combined set of prime factors be the finite set \(K\). By the conclusion above, all subsequent key terms \(x\) satisfy

\[P(x) \subseteq K.\]

Since \(K\) has only finitely many subsets, and different key terms must have different sets of prime factors, the total number of key terms is finite. Let all key terms be

\[b_1, b_2, \dots, b_s,\]

and define

\[d_j = \prod_{p \in P(b_j)} p = \operatorname{rad}(b_j) \quad (1 \le j \le s). ag{6}\]

By the definition of key terms and property (3), for any \(m \ge a_1\),

\[m \in \mathcal{A} \iff \exists j \in \{1, \dots, s\}, \quad d_j \mid m. ag{7}\]

Let

\[L = \operatorname{lcm}(d_1, d_2, \dots, d_s). ag{8}\]

Since each \(d_j \mid L\), by (7) we get

\[m \in \mathcal{A} \iff m + L \in \mathcal{A} \quad (m \ge a_1). ag{9}\]

Finally, let

\[T = \#(\mathcal{A} \cap [a_1, a_1 + L)). ag{10}\]

By (9), the map \(m \mapsto m + L\) gives an order-preserving bijection from \(\mathcal{A}\) to \(\mathcal{A} \cap [a_1 + L, \infty)\). Therefore, after removing the first \(T\) terms, the remaining terms are

\[a_1 + L, \quad a_2 + L, \quad a_3 + L, \dots\]

Thus, for every positive integer \(n\),

\[a_{n+T} = a_n + L.\]

Hence proved.

\[ oxed{ ext{There exist positive integers } T ext{ and } L ext{ such that } a_{n+T} = a_n + L.}\]
